subject: Civil Engineering
title: Railways: Track and Alignment
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Railways: Track and Alignment.

hook.text: A train can't climb steep hills or make sharp turns. The track must be almost flat and straight.

buildup.text: Rail grades rarely exceed 2%. Curves use large radii — ten times wider than highway curves.

discovery.text: Cant tilts the outer rail higher on curves — the same principle as road superelevation.

twist.text: Transition curves ease from straight to curved — preventing jerky lateral acceleration.

climax.text: Japan's Shinkansen runs at 200 mph on continuously welded rail — no joints, no bumps.

punchline.text: Smooth track means fast trains. Every millimeter matters.

quiz.question: Why are railway curves designed with much larger radii than road curves?
options: Trains are heavier and need more space to turn safely at speed
Railways are built in flat terrain only
Larger curves reduce the amount of rail material needed

details.summary: Railway track engineering encompasses the design of rail, sleepers (ties), ballast, and subgrade that support train loads and guide wheels along the alignment. Track geometry must maintain precise gauge, cant (superelevation), and alignment to ensure safe high-speed operation and passenger comfort.
details.whyItMatters: Railways are the most energy-efficient land transportation mode, moving freight at one-quarter the energy cost of trucks. Well-engineered track enables reliable high-capacity service for centuries.
takeaways: Standard gauge of 1,435 mm is used by about 60% of the world's railways
Ballast distributes wheel loads and provides drainage beneath the track structure
Cant tilts the track in curves to balance centrifugal force on trains

faq.question: Why is track gauge so important and why isn't it standardized worldwide?
faq.answer: Gauge determines which trains can run on which tracks. Different countries adopted different gauges in early railway history for various strategic and technical reasons. Russia chose 1,520 mm partly to prevent invasion by rail.

faq.question: What is ballastless slab track and when is it used?
faq.answer: Slab track replaces ballast with a concrete slab that supports the rails directly. It costs more initially but requires almost no maintenance, making it ideal for tunnels, bridges, and high-speed lines where maintenance access is difficult. Most modern high-speed railways use slab track.
